# Characters and strings

A character is an atom, like a number. A string is a vector of characters. Single quotes write one character, and double quotes write a string of any length, even one character or none.

```bpl
⍴'a'               ⍝ ⍬ₓ
⍴"a"               ⍝ [1]ₓ
⍴"abc"             ⍝ [3]ₓ
⍴""                ⍝ [0]ₓ
```

## Quotes inside text

The character literal for a single quote is `'''`. A string can hold an apostrophe as it is. To put a double quote inside a string, write it twice.

```bpl
•ucs '''           ⍝ 39ₓ
≢"can't"           ⍝ 5ₓ
≢"say ""hi"""      ⍝ 8ₓ
```

## Strands of text

Literals separated by spaces form a strand, which is one vector. Characters side by side form a string. Strings side by side form a vector of strings. So `"x" "y"` is two strings, and `'x' 'y'` is the one string `"xy"`.

```bpl
'a' 'b' 'c'        ⍝ "abc"
≢"one" "three"     ⍝ 2ₓ
≢¨"one" "three"    ⍝ [3 5]ₓ
```

A vector of strings is how keys are written, as in `"x" "y":1 2`. [Axis keys](keyed.qmd) covers keyed arrays.

## How text displays

A string on its own displays as its text, and a character matrix displays one row per line. Inside a larger array, strings show in double quotes and characters in single quotes, so you can tell them apart. In the REPL:

```text
      "abc"
abc
      2 3⍴"abcdef"
abc
def
      ⊂"ab"
⊂"ab"
      "abc",⊂"de"
'a' 'b' 'c' "de"
```

## Working with text

Functions that work on vectors work on strings. `=` compares character by character, and `≡` compares whole strings. Search functions find characters or patterns, and Grade sorts characters by code point.

```bpl
"abc"="abd"        ⍝ $t $t $f
"abc"≡"abc"        ⍝ $t
"abc"⍳"cz"         ⍝ [2 3]ₓ
"an"⍷"banana"      ⍝ $f $t $f $t $f $f
[⍋"bca"]⌷"bca"     ⍝ "abc"
⌽"abc"             ⍝ "cba"
```

Adding an integer to a character moves it along the Unicode code points. Subtracting one character from another gives the distance between them. `<` and the other order comparisons take only numbers.

```bpl
'a'+3              ⍝ 'd'
'a'+⍳3             ⍝ "abc"
'd'-'a'            ⍝ 3ₓ
```

[System functions](system-functions.qmd) cover the rest of text handling. `•ucs` converts between characters and code points, `•c` changes case, and `•a` and `•d` hold the alphabet and the digits. `⍕` formats values as text, and `•r` matches regular expressions, as [Regular expressions](regex.ipynb) shows.

```bpl
•ucs "ABC"         ⍝ [65 66 67]ₓ
•c "Hello"         ⍝ "hello"
"a2b"∊•d           ⍝ $f $t $f
⍕3.5 2             ⍝ "3.5 2"
```
